## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Eḷakalomadhovāpana Sutta* (Bhikkhu Vibhaṅga Nissaggiya Pācittiya 17) sets forth the disciplinary rule prohibiting a Buddhist monk from having an unordained or unrelated nun wash, dye, or comb unspun sheep's wool (*eḷakaloma*) [SuttaCentral]. Under this training rule, any monk who induces a nun to perform such tasks incurs an offense requiring forfeiture of the wool and formal confession [SuttaCentral]. Modern translations of the text include an English rendering by Bhikkhu Brahmali among five translations in five languages recorded on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].

This monastic precept is widely attested across early Buddhist traditions [SuttaCentral]. Curated parallels cataloged by SuttaCentral include the corresponding Pali Bhikkhu Pātimokkha rule and the Bhikkhu Parivāra (Np 17), as well as Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa and Vibhaṅga counterparts in the Sarvāstivāda, Mūlasarvāstivāda (extant in Sanskrit, Classical Chinese, and Classical Tibetan), Mahīśāsaka (Np 27), Mahāsāṅghika and Lokottaravāda (Np 17), Dharmaguptaka, Kāśyapīya, and the Chinese *Upāliparipṛcchā* [SuttaCentral].

DharmaNexus identifies extensive internal reuse within the Pali canon, registering 600 matching passages across 107 texts [DharmaNexus]. Due to standardized legal frameworks, interrogative formulas, and word analysis (*padabhājana*), substantial textual overlaps occur with adjacent rules regarding clothing and interactions with nuns, notably Nissaggiya Pācittiya 4 (§1.19–2.47 sharing over 6,000 characters with §1.30–2.2.27), Nissaggiya Pācittiya 5, 6, 8, 9, 26, and 27, Pācittiya 23, 25, and 26, and sections of the Khandhakas (such as the *Bhesajjakkhandhaka* [Kd 6] and *Bhikkhunikkhandhaka* [Kd 20]) [DharmaNexus]. Beyond Pali, DharmaNexus algorithmically aligns passages of the text with Tibetan vinaya literature—including the *Bhikṣuṇīvinayavibhaṅga* (D0005) and the *Vinayakārikā* (D4123)—as well as fragments of the Sanskrit *Saṅgītisūtra* [DharmaNexus].

*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
